newsitem.title: UK: Churchill letters sell for three times estimate.
newsitem.headline: Churchill letters sell for three times estimate.

text.p: Handwritten letters from Winston Churchill to his younger brother Jack fighting in World War One were auctioned off for more than a quarter of a million pounds on Thursday.

Eighteen letters by Britain's most famous 20th-century statesman, many marked "secret" or "private", fetched a total of 252,380 pounds ($423,000) - three times what the Sotheby's auctioneers expected - when they went under the hammer in London.
Nearly all the letters were bought by The Fine Arts Society Plc on behalf of American publishing magnate Steve Forbes, a keen collector of Churchill memorabilia.
"It's nice to have a clean sweep," said Fine Arts Society director Simon Edsor, who battled hard against a Turkish bidder to snap up 12 of the letters.
"It's a very important group - the letters are as close to Churchill as you can get in an important period of his life."
Forbes, best known as editor-in-chief of Forbes magazine, stood as a Republican presidential candidate in the last United States election.
Addressed to "my dearest Jack", a soldier in the British forces, Churchill's letters date from August 1914, just three weeks after the start of World War One.
Experts rate them as especially valuable since they describe Winston Churchill's most personal feelings about the war, its leaders and their policies.
Edsor paid 47,000 pounds for a nine-page letter signed "yours always, W" in which Churchill discusses events leading to the fateful Dardanelles offensive of World War One.
Churchill was Britain's first lord of the admiralty at the time of the Dardanelles campaign and prime minister a generation later during World War Two. He died in 1965 at the age of 90.
Churchill's brainchild, the campaign was intended to break through Turkey and open up a southern front against Germany.

"Most of the Unionists are now fully convinced...of the obligation to carry the Dardanelles policy through," Churchill wrote, "but I have had a hard battle all these weeks and have been fighting every inch of the road."
But the plan failed dramatically when it failed to surprise the enemy forces, who launched a counter-attack that left more than 28,000 dead and 96,000 injured on the British side.

Two other letters focusing on the campaign were bought by the Turkish bidder for 48,000 and 46,000 pounds on behalf of the armed forces in Ankara, who pipped Edsor to the post after a bout of aggressive bidding.
The Turkish bidder said the letters would be put on display at the Galibolu Museum in the Dardanelles in a collection dedicated to soldiers that lost their lives there.
